blocks.text: Absolute electrode potentials cannot be measured because of the formation of an electrical double layer when an element is placed in a solution of its ions. When zinc is placed in a solution containing zinc ions, a tiny number of zinc atoms on the surface are converted to zinc ions, which go into solution, leaving an excess of electrons on the surface of the zinc. The solution around the metal now has excess Zn2+ ions, and some of these cations near the surface are attracted to it, so an electrical double layer is formed. This build-up of charge causes an electric potential (voltage) between the metal and the metal ions in solution (Figure 10.3).

blocks.alt: A zinc rod dips into ZnSO4 (aq). Down both faces of the rod inside the solution are negative charges (electrons), and facing them on each side is a column of circles marked +2, labelled Zinc(II) ions.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.3: Formation of electrical double layer (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.3).

blocks.text: Because of the double layer the potential cannot be measured directly, but the difference in potential between the metal/metal ion system and another system can be measured. This value is the electrode potential, E, measured in volts; the system used for comparison is the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE).
